claim: In 2016/2017, Washington State experienced a mumps outbreak despite high childhood vaccination rates.
source: In 2016/2017, Washington State experienced a mumps outbreak despite high childhood vaccination rates, with cases more frequently detected among school-aged children and members of the Marshallese community.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data presented throughout the manuscript showing vaccination rates and case counts.

claim: Cases were more frequently detected among school-aged children during the Washington State mumps outbreak.
source: In 2016/2017, Washington State experienced a mumps outbreak despite high childhood vaccination rates, with cases more frequently detected among school-aged children and members of the Marshallese community.
evidence: The abstract states this and it is supported by epidemiological data showing highest incidence among children aged 10-19.

claim: Cases were more frequently detected among members of the Marshallese community during the Washington State mumps outbreak.
source: In 2016/2017, Washington State experienced a mumps outbreak despite high childhood vaccination rates, with cases more frequently detected among school-aged children and members of the Marshallese community.
evidence: The abstract states this and it is supported by data showing 52% of cases were Marshallese despite comprising only 0.3% of the population.

claim: 166 mumps virus genomes were sequenced from Washington and other US states.
source: We sequenced 166 mumps virus genomes collected in Washington and other US states, and traced mumps introductions and transmission within Washington.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and confirmed in the methods section.

claim: Mumps was introduced into Washington approximately 13 times.
source: We uncover that mumps was introduced into Washington approximately 13 times, primarily from Arkansas, sparking multiple co-circulating transmission chains.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic analysis showing the distribution of introductions (Figure 3b).

claim: Mumps introductions into Washington were primarily from Arkansas.
source: We uncover that mumps was introduced into Washington approximately 13 times, primarily from Arkansas, sparking multiple co-circulating transmission chains.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by phylogeographic reconstruction showing Arkansas as the source of most introductions.

claim: The mumps outbreak in Washington was overwhelmingly sustained by transmission within the Marshallese community.
source: Instead, the outbreak in Washington was overwhelmingly sustained by transmission within the Marshallese community.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structured coalescent analyses showing most internal nodes inferred as Marshallese.

claim: Contact networks are critical for mumps transmission.
source: Our findings underscore the utility of genomic data to clarify epidemiologic factors driving transmission and pinpoint contact networks as critical for mumps transmission.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion drawn from the phylogenetic and epidemiological analyses.

claim: Contact structures and historic disparities may leave populations at increased risk for respiratory virus disease even when a vaccine is effective and widely used.
source: These results imply that contact structures and historic disparities may leave populations at increased risk for respiratory virus disease even when a vaccine is effective and widely used.
evidence: This is stated as an implication in the abstract based on the findings about transmission within the Marshallese community.

claim: Washington State reported 889 confirmed and probable mumps cases in 2016/2017.
source: Washington State was heavily affected, reporting 889 confirmed and probable cases.
evidence: This is directly stated in the introduction and represents surveillance data.

claim: Mumps vaccine-induced immunity wanes over 13–30 years.
source: Longitudinal studies (Davidkin et al., 2008), epidemiologic outbreak investigations (Cardemil et al., 2017), and epidemic models (Lewnard and Grad, 2018) suggest that mumps vaccine-induced immunity wanes over 13–30 years, consistent with the preponderance of young adult cases in recent outbreaks.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Most Washington mumps cases in 2016/17 were vaccinated.
source: Like with other recent mumps outbreaks, most Washington cases in 2016/17 were vaccinated.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data showing >90% of school-aged cases had received two doses of MMR vaccine.

claim: Incidence in Washington was highest among children aged 10–18 years.
source: Unusually though, while most US outbreaks in 2016/2017 were associated with university settings (Albertson et al., 2016; Bonwitt et al., 2017; Donahue et al., 2017; Golwalkar et al., 2018; Iowa Mumps Outbreak Response Team et al., 2018; Wohl et al., 2020), incidence in Washington was highest among children aged 10–18 years, younger than expected given waning immunity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by epidemiological data in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: Approximately 52% of the total mumps cases in Washington were Marshallese.
source: The outbreak was also peculiar in that approximately 52% of the total cases were Marshallese, an ethnic community that comprises ~0.3% of Washington's population.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by surveillance data.

claim: The Marshallese community comprises approximately 0.3% of Washington's population.
source: The outbreak was also peculiar in that approximately 52% of the total cases were Marshallese, an ethnic community that comprises ~0.3% of Washington's population.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as demographic information.

claim: Of the 2954 confirmed and probable Arkansas mumps cases, 57% were Marshallese.
source: Of the 2954 confirmed and probable Arkansas cases, 57% were Marshallese, and 57% of cases were children aged 5–17 (Fields et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Fields et al., 2019.

claim: 57% of Arkansas mumps cases were children aged 5–17.
source: Of the 2954 confirmed and probable Arkansas cases, 57% were Marshallese, and 57% of cases were children aged 5–17 (Fields et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Fields et al., 2019.

claim: Among infected school-aged children in Arkansas and Washington, >90% had previously received two doses of MMR vaccine.
source: Among the infected school-aged children in Arkansas and Washington, >90% had previously received two doses of MMR vaccine (Fields et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Fields et al., 2019.

claim: Between 1947 and 1986, the United States occupied the Republic of Marshall Islands.
source: Between 1947 and 1986, the United States occupied the Republic of Marshall Islands and detonated the equivalent of >7000 Hiroshima size nuclear bombs as part of its nuclear testing program (Barker, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Barker, 2012.

claim: The United States detonated the equivalent of >7000 Hiroshima size nuclear bombs in the Marshall Islands as part of its nuclear testing program.
source: Between 1947 and 1986, the United States occupied the Republic of Marshall Islands and detonated the equivalent of >7000 Hiroshima size nuclear bombs as part of its nuclear testing program (Barker, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Barker, 2012.

claim: US nuclear testing in the Marshall Islands precipitated widespread environmental destruction, nuclear contamination, and dire health consequences.
source: The effects were devastating, precipitating widespread environmental destruction, nuclear contamination, and dire health consequences (Hallgren et al., 2015; Niedenthal, 1997; Palafox et al., 2007; Simon, 1997; Takahashi et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Marshallese individuals inhabiting the targeted atolls were forcibly moved to other islands.
source: Marshallese individuals inhabiting the targeted atolls were forcibly moved to other islands, and many were exposed to nuclear fallout (Abella et al., 2019) that persists on the Islands today (Bordner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Abella et al., 2019 and Bordner et al., 2016.

claim: Many Marshallese individuals were exposed to nuclear fallout.
source: Marshallese individuals inhabiting the targeted atolls were forcibly moved to other islands, and many were exposed to nuclear fallout (Abella et al., 2019) that persists on the Islands today (Bordner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Abella et al., 2019 and Bordner et al., 2016.

claim: Nuclear fallout persists on the Marshall Islands today.
source: Marshallese individuals inhabiting the targeted atolls were forcibly moved to other islands, and many were exposed to nuclear fallout (Abella et al., 2019) that persists on the Islands today (Bordner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Bordner et al., 2016.

claim: Marshallese individuals living on and off the Islands experience significant health disparities including a higher burden from infectious diseases and chronic health conditions.
source: Marshallese individuals living on and off the Islands experience significant health disparities including a higher burden from infectious diseases and chronic health conditions (Adams et al., 1986; Wong et al., 1979; Yamada et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to multiple studies.

claim: From 1996 to 2020, Marshallese individuals were specifically excluded from Medicaid eligibility despite legal residency in the US permitted under the Compact of Free Association (COFA) Treaty.
source: Compounding these disparities, from 1996 to 2020 (Hirono, 2019), Marshallese individuals were specifically excluded from Medicaid eligibility despite legal residency in the US permitted under the Compact of Free Association (COFA) Treaty.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Hirono, 2019.

claim: Many US-residing Marshallese are uninsured, with poor access to healthcare.
source: As a result, many US-residing Marshallese are uninsured, with poor access to healthcare (McElfish et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to McElfish et al., 2015.

claim: Marshallese households are more likely to be multigenerational and tend to be larger on average.
source: Marshallese households are more likely to be multigenerational and tend to be larger on average (Harris and Jones, 2005; US Census Bureau, 2021), potentially increasing the number and intensity of interactions among individuals.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Harris and Jones, 2005 and US Census Bureau, 2021.

claim: Larger household size potentially increases the number and intensity of interactions among individuals.
source: Marshallese households are more likely to be multigenerational and tend to be larger on average (Harris and Jones, 2005; US Census Bureau, 2021), potentially increasing the number and intensity of interactions among individuals.
evidence: This is stated as a potential consequence in the introduction, representing an inference from the household size data.

claim: 110 mumps viral genomes were obtained from specimens collected from laboratory-confirmed mumps cases in Washington State.
source: We sequenced 110 mumps viral genomes obtained from specimens collected from laboratory-confirmed mumps cases in Washington State and another 56 from other US states collected between 2006 and 2018.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents the study's data collection.

claim: 56 mumps viral genomes were obtained from other US states collected between 2006 and 2018.
source: We sequenced 110 mumps viral genomes obtained from specimens collected from laboratory-confirmed mumps cases in Washington State and another 56 from other US states collected between 2006 and 2018.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents the study's data collection.

claim: The Washington State outbreak began in October 2016.
source: The Washington State outbreak began in October 2016 and peaked in winter of 2017, culminating in 889 confirmed and probable cases across Washington (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The Washington State mumps outbreak peaked in winter of 2017.
source: The Washington State outbreak began in October 2016 and peaked in winter of 2017, culminating in 889 confirmed and probable cases across Washington (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Individuals aged <1 to 64 years were affected by the Washington mumps outbreak.
source: Individuals aged <1 to 64 years were affected, but incidence was highest among children aged 10–14 (44.9 cases per 100,000) and 15–19 (47.0 per 100,000) (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Incidence was highest among children aged 10–14 (44.9 cases per 100,000) in the Washington mumps outbreak.
source: Individuals aged <1 to 64 years were affected, but incidence was highest among children aged 10–14 (44.9 cases per 100,000) and 15–19 (47.0 per 100,000) (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Incidence was highest among children aged 15–19 (47.0 per 100,000) in the Washington mumps outbreak.
source: Individuals aged <1 to 64 years were affected, but incidence was highest among children aged 10–14 (44.9 cases per 100,000) and 15–19 (47.0 per 100,000) (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Among outbreak cases 5–19 years of age, 91% of individuals were considered up-to-date on mumps vaccine.
source: Among outbreak cases 5–19 years of age, 91% of individuals were considered up-to-date on mumps vaccine.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and represents surveillance data.

claim: Adults aged 20–39 years were infected at a rate of 12.9 cases per 100,000 in the Washington mumps outbreak.
source: Adults in the age group most likely to be parents of school aged children (20–39 years old) were infected at a rate of only 12.9 cases per 100,000, but comprised a significant proportion (29%) of total cases (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Adults aged 20–39 years comprised 29% of total mumps cases in Washington.
source: Adults in the age group most likely to be parents of school aged children (20–39 years old) were infected at a rate of only 12.9 cases per 100,000, but comprised a significant proportion (29%) of total cases (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Among Marshallese cases aged 5–19, 93% were up-to-date on vaccination.
source: Among Marshallese cases aged 5–19, 93% were up-to-date on vaccination, suggesting that this over-representation is not attributable to poor vaccine coverage.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and represents surveillance data.

claim: The over-representation of Marshallese cases is not attributable to poor vaccine coverage.
source: Among Marshallese cases aged 5–19, 93% were up-to-date on vaccination, suggesting that this over-representation is not attributable to poor vaccine coverage.
evidence: This is stated as an inference in the results section based on the high vaccination rate among Marshallese cases.

claim: Nine Washington sequences were highly divergent from other North American genotype G viruses, with a time to the most recent common ancestor (TMRCA) of ~22 years.
source: Nine Washington sequences were highly divergent from other North American genotype G viruses, with a time to the most recent common ancestor (TMRCA) of ~22 years (Figure 2, blue tips with long branches clustered toward the top of the tree).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Seven of the divergent Washington sequences cluster with viruses sampled from New Zealand.
source: Seven of these divergent Washington sequences cluster with viruses sampled from New Zealand (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggesting they could be travel-related.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The divergent Washington sequences that cluster with New Zealand viruses could be travel-related.
source: Seven of these divergent Washington sequences cluster with viruses sampled from New Zealand (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggesting they could be travel-related.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion in the results section based on phylogenetic clustering.

claim: The remaining Washington sequences nest within the diversity of other North American viruses, and descend from the same mumps lineage that has circulated in North America since 2006.
source: The remaining Washington sequences nest within the diversity of other North American viruses, and descend from the same mumps lineage that has circulated in North America since 2006 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Most British Columbia sequences form a distinct cluster on a long branch.
source: Despite the close geographic proximity between British Columbia and Washington, most British Columbia sequences form a distinct cluster on a long branch (Figure 2), suggesting seeding from an unsampled location.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The distinct British Columbia cluster suggests seeding from an unsampled location.
source: Despite the close geographic proximity between British Columbia and Washington, most British Columbia sequences form a distinct cluster on a long branch (Figure 2), suggesting seeding from an unsampled location.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion in the results section based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Most Washington viruses cluster within a clade of viruses sampled in Arkansas.
source: Although viruses from Washington are scattered throughout the phylogeny, most cluster within a clade of viruses sampled in Arkansas (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: One sample from Wisconsin in 2006 grouped with genotype A viruses.
source: One sample from Wisconsin in 2006 grouped with genotype A viruses, another sample from Wisconsin in 2015 grouped with genotype H viruses, and one sample from Washington in 2017 grouped with genotype K viruses (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: One sample from Wisconsin in 2015 grouped with genotype H viruses.
source: One sample from Wisconsin in 2006 grouped with genotype A viruses, another sample from Wisconsin in 2015 grouped with genotype H viruses, and one sample from Washington in 2017 grouped with genotype K viruses (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: One sample from Washington in 2017 grouped with genotype K viruses.
source: One sample from Wisconsin in 2006 grouped with genotype A viruses, another sample from Wisconsin in 2015 grouped with genotype H viruses, and one sample from Washington in 2017 grouped with genotype K viruses (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Washington genotype K virus is closely related to a genotype K mumps virus collected during a mumps outbreak in Massachusetts from an individual who reported international travel.
source: The Washington genotype K virus (Washington.USA/9.17/FH94/K) is closely related to a genotype K mumps virus collected during a mumps outbreak in Massachusetts from an individual who reported international travel (Wohl et al., 2020; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to Wohl et al., 2020 and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The primary outbreak clade was introduced from Arkansas to Washington around August 2016.
source: We refer to the largest cluster as the 'primary outbreak clade', and infer its introduction from Arkansas to Washington around August 2016 (August 7, 2016, 95% HPD: July 11, 2016 to September 19, 2016, Figure 3b), 3.5 months before Washington's first reported case.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3b and represents phylogenetic inference.

claim: The primary outbreak clade was introduced 3.5 months before Washington's first reported case.
source: We refer to the largest cluster as the 'primary outbreak clade', and infer its introduction from Arkansas to Washington around August 2016 (August 7, 2016, 95% HPD: July 11, 2016 to September 19, 2016, Figure 3b), 3.5 months before Washington's first reported case.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and represents phylogenetic inference compared to surveillance data.

claim: Four introductions from Arkansas account for 92/110 sequenced cases.
source: In contrast, four introductions from Arkansas account for 92/110 sequenced cases, suggesting that these introductions led to more sustained chains of transmission following introduction (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3b.

claim: Arkansas introductions led to more sustained chains of transmission following introduction.
source: In contrast, four introductions from Arkansas account for 92/110 sequenced cases, suggesting that these introductions led to more sustained chains of transmission following introduction (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion in the results section based on the number of cases associated with Arkansas introductions.

claim: Almost all North American SH genes were identical, resulting in a single, large polytomy.
source: Almost all North American SH genes were identical, resulting in a single, large polytomy (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: SH sequences lack sufficient resolution to elucidate fine-grained patterns of geographic spread.
source: This indicates that SH sequences lack sufficient resolution to elucidate fine-grained patterns of geographic spread, consistent with previous findings (Gouma et al., 2016; Wohl et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the SH gene analysis, with citations to previous studies.

claim: Marshallese cases were significantly more likely to be basal than non-Marshallese cases (odds ratio = 3.2, p=0.00725).
source: However, we do find evidence for community status as a strong predictor for being basal on the phylogeny. Marshallese cases were significantly more likely to be basal than non-Marshallese cases (odds ratio = 3.2, p=0.00725, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Table 1, representing statistical analysis.

claim: 27% (14/52) of non-Marshallese tips were ancestral to downstream samples.
source: While only 27% (14/52) of non-Marshallese tips were ancestral to downstream samples, 56% (32/57) of Marshallese tips were ancestral in lineages with sampled propagated transmission (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: 56% (32/57) of Marshallese tips were ancestral in lineages with sampled propagated transmission.
source: While only 27% (14/52) of non-Marshallese tips were ancestral to downstream samples, 56% (32/57) of Marshallese tips were ancestral in lineages with sampled propagated transmission (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Community membership was a significant determinant of sustained transmission while controlling for vaccination status and age.
source: These results suggest that community membership was a significant determinant of sustained transmission while controlling for vaccination status and age.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the logistic regression analysis.

claim: Every introduction that was not seeded from Arkansas led to exclusively non-Marshallese infections.
source: Every introduction that was not seeded from Arkansas led to exclusively non-Marshallese infections, while introductions from Arkansas defined lineages that circulated for longer and were enriched with Marshallese tips (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Introductions from Arkansas defined lineages that circulated for longer and were enriched with Marshallese tips.
source: Every introduction that was not seeded from Arkansas led to exclusively non-Marshallese infections, while introductions from Arkansas defined lineages that circulated for longer and were enriched with Marshallese tips (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Of 88 internal nodes, 74 were inferred to circulate within the Marshallese community with posterior probability of at least 0.95.
source: Of 88 internal nodes, 74 were inferred to circulate within the Marshallese community with posterior probability of at least 0.95 (Figure 5a,b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5a,b.

claim: Movement of a lineage from the Marshallese deme into the non-Marshallese deme subsequently caused the lineage to die out quickly.
source: Movement of a lineage from the Marshallese deme into the non-Marshallese deme subsequently caused the lineage to die out quickly (Figure 5a, dark blue branches).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Within the primary outbreak clade, 29 transmission events from Marshallese to non-Marshallese groups were estimated (95% HPD: 21, 37).
source: We estimate substantially more transmission from Marshallese to non-Marshallese groups than the opposite: within the primary outbreak clade, we estimate 29 transmission events from Marshallese to non-Marshallese groups (95% HPD: 21, 37), and only 6 (95% HPD: 0, 14) from non-Marshallese to Marshallese groups (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Within the primary outbreak clade, 6 transmission events from non-Marshallese to Marshallese groups were estimated (95% HPD: 0, 14).
source: We estimate substantially more transmission from Marshallese to non-Marshallese groups than the opposite: within the primary outbreak clade, we estimate 29 transmission events from Marshallese to non-Marshallese groups (95% HPD: 21, 37), and only 6 (95% HPD: 0, 14) from non-Marshallese to Marshallese groups (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Transmission predominantly occurred in one direction: transmission events leading to non-Marshallese infections usually died out and did not typically re-seed circulation within the Marshallese community.
source: This strongly suggests that transmission predominantly occurred in one direction: transmission events leading to non-Marshallese infections usually died out and did not typically re-seed circulation within the Marshallese community.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the structured coalescent analysis.

claim: The effective population size (Ne) for the non-Marshallese group is approximately three times higher than that of the Marshallese group.
source: While the total number of Marshallese and non-Marshallese cases reported through the public health surveillance system were similar (Supplementary file 1b), we estimate that Ne for the non-Marshallese group is approximately three times higher than that of the Marshallese group.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on structured coalescent model estimates.

claim: Lower effective population sizes suggest higher transmission rates, assuming the same number of infected individuals in each group.
source: Assuming the same number of infected individuals in each group, lower Ne's suggest higher transmission rates (Volz, 2012), suggesting more transmission within the Marshallese deme.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to Volz, 2012.

claim: The outbreak was primarily sustained by transmission within the Marshallese community.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that the outbreak was primarily sustained by transmission within the Marshallese community.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Spillover into the non-Marshallese community occurred, but transmission was generally not as successful there, resulting in short, terminal transmission chains.
source: While we do observe spillover into the non-Marshallese community, transmission was generally not as successful there, resulting in short, terminal transmission chains.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Not up-to-date individuals are dispersed throughout the phylogeny and do not cluster together.
source: The not up-to-date individuals present in our data set are dispersed throughout the phylogeny and do not cluster together (Figure 7), suggesting that there is no genetic difference between viruses infecting individuals with different vaccination statuses.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 7.

claim: There is no genetic difference between viruses infecting individuals with different vaccination statuses.
source: The not up-to-date individuals present in our data set are dispersed throughout the phylogeny and do not cluster together (Figure 7), suggesting that there is no genetic difference between viruses infecting individuals with different vaccination statuses.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion in the results section based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Social networks can be critical determinants of mumps transmission.
source: However, our data do suggest that social networks can be critical determinants of mumps transmission.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion section based on the study's findings.

claim: Mumps has historically caused outbreaks in communities with strong, interconnected contact patterns.
source: Mumps has historically caused outbreaks in communities with strong, interconnected contact patterns (Barskey et al., 2012; Fields et al., 2019; Nelson et al., 2013), and in dense housing environments (Snijders et al., 2012), highlighted most recently by outbreaks in US detention centers (Lo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Mumps has historically caused outbreaks in dense housing environments.
source: Mumps has historically caused outbreaks in communities with strong, interconnected contact patterns (Barskey et al., 2012; Fields et al., 2019; Nelson et al., 2013), and in dense housing environments (Snijders et al., 2012), highlighted most recently by outbreaks in US detention centers (Lo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations to multiple studies.

claim: In 2016, most mumps outbreaks in the US were associated with university settings.
source: In 2016, most outbreaks in the US were associated with university settings (Albertson et al., 2016; Bonwitt et al., 2017; Donahue et al., 2017; Golwalkar et al., 2018; Iowa Mumps Outbreak Response Team et al., 2018; Wohl et al., 2020), including a separate, smaller outbreak in Washington State associated with Greek housing (Bonwitt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Provision of an outbreak dose of mumps-containing vaccine to high-risk groups may be especially effective for limiting mumps transmission in future outbreaks.
source: Provision of an outbreak dose of mumps-containing vaccine to high-risk groups may therefore be especially effective for limiting mumps transmission in future outbreaks.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation in the discussion section based on the study's findings and previous literature.

claim: Others have reported success in using outbreak dose mumps vaccinations to reduce mumps transmission on college campuses.
source: Others have reported success in using outbreak dose mumps vaccinations to reduce mumps transmission on college campuses (Cardemil et al., 2017; Iowa Mumps Outbreak Response Team et al., 2018) and in the US army (Arday et al., 1989; Eick et al., 2008; Green, 2006; Kelley et al., 1991), and the CDC currently recommends providing outbreak vaccine doses to individuals with increased risk due to an outbreak (Marlow et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations to multiple studies.

claim: The CDC currently recommends providing outbreak vaccine doses to individuals with increased risk due to an outbreak.
source: Others have reported success in using outbreak dose mumps vaccinations to reduce mumps transmission on college campuses (Cardemil et al., 2017; Iowa Mumps Outbreak Response Team et al., 2018) and in the US army (Arday et al., 1989; Eick et al., 2008; Green, 2006; Kelley et al., 1991), and the CDC currently recommends providing outbreak vaccine doses to individuals with increased risk due to an outbreak (Marlow et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation to Marlow et al., 2020.

claim: Multigenerational living is common in the Marshallese community.
source: Multigenerational living is common in the Marshallese community (Fields et al., 2019), and Marshallese households tend to be larger on average (average household size = 5.28 (Harris and Jones, 2005), average household size for entire US populace = 2.52 US Census Bureau, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations to Fields et al., 2019, Harris and Jones, 2005, and US Census Bureau, 2021.

claim: The average Marshallese household size is 5.28.
source: Multigenerational living is common in the Marshallese community (Fields et al., 2019), and Marshallese households tend to be larger on average (average household size = 5.28 (Harris and Jones, 2005), average household size for entire US populace = 2.52 US Census Bureau, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation to Harris and Jones, 2005.

claim: The average household size for the entire US populace is 2.52.
source: Multigenerational living is common in the Marshallese community (Fields et al., 2019), and Marshallese households tend to be larger on average (average household size = 5.28 (Harris and Jones, 2005), average household size for entire US populace = 2.52 US Census Bureau, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation to US Census Bureau, 2021.

claim: The Marshallese community is often described as close-knit, with frequent and close interactions among individuals, a strong sense of community, and a broader sense of family than the single-family unit typical of broader American culture.
source: The Marshallese community is often described as close-knit, with frequent and close interactions among individuals, a strong sense of community, and a broader sense of family than the single-family unit typical of broader American culture (Barker, 2012; Embassy of the Republic of the Marshall Islands to the United States of America, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations to Barker, 2012 and Embassy of the Republic of the Marshall Islands to the United States of America, 2021.

claim: Infection intensity within the Marshallese community may have been exacerbated by low rates of insurance coverage and poor access to healthcare.
source: It is also possible that infection intensity within the Marshallese community was exacerbated by low rates of insurance coverage and poor access to healthcare (McElfish et al., 2017; Towne et al., 2021), hesitancy to seek medical care (Williams and Hampton, 2005), and health disparities stemming from US occupation, nuclear testing, and exclusion from healthcare services.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility in the discussion section with citations to multiple studies.

claim: The US signed the Compact of Free Association Treaty (COFA) with the Marshall Islands in 1989, permitting Marshallese residents to live and work in the US without visas.
source: As part of reparations for US nuclear testing, the US signed the Compact of Free Association Treaty (COFA)(Congress 108th United States, 2003) with the Marshall Islands in 1989, permitting Marshallese residents to live and work in the US without visas.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation to Congress 108th United States, 2003.

claim: Eligibility for Medicaid was revoked for COFA immigrants in 1996.
source: However, eligibility for Medicaid was revoked for COFA immigrants in 1996, and US-residing Marshallese remain economically disadvantaged and under-insured (McElfish, 2016; McElfish et al., 2017, McElfish et al., 2015).
